sentences.text: Achillobator was a large, heavily built, bipedal carnivore that likely hunted using an enlarged sickle claw on its second toe.
This animal measured approximately 4.5 to 5 meters in length and weighed between 250 and 350 kilograms.
Its skull featured a deep, robust maxilla measuring about 29 centimeters, while the coracoid bone was broad and 16.7 centimeters long.
The holotype specimen preserved a left maxilla with teeth, vertebrae, a nearly complete pelvic girdle, leg bones, arm bones, ribs, and tail elements.
Achillobator is one of the largest known raptors, rivaling in size with the North American Utahraptor.
Although the holotype lacked feather traces, evidence from relatives suggests Achillobator likely had plumage.
The first remains of Achillobator were discovered in 1989 during a Mongolian-Soviet field expedition and formally described in 1999.
The genus Achillobator was named by Perle, Norell, and Clark in 1999.
A large, mostly disarticulated partial theropod skeleton was found about 5.6 km from the main locality in the Burkhant locality of the Bayan Shireh Formation.
The animal likely hunted using an enlarged sickle claw on its second toe.
The robust maxilla of Achillobator suggests it hunted large prey.
Achillobator's stocky build and short legs suggest it was not adapted for high-speed running.
Research by Perle and team in 1999 suggested that Achillobator had massive thighs and robust legs suited for moderate fast-running.
In 2009, Manning and team analyzed the biomechanics of dromaeosaurid sickle claws to test their function regarding stress distribution.
Manning and team found that dromaeosaurid sickle claws were ideal for both climbing and a ground-dwelling lifestyle.
Achillobator shared its environment with theropods including the therizinosaurs Erlikosaurus and Segnosaurus, the ornithomimosaur Garudimimus, and the tyrannosauroid Khankhuuluu.
The large, long-necked sauropod Erketu was also found in the same formation as Achillobator.
Ornithischians found in the same formation included the ankylosaurs Talarurus and Tsagantegia, the marginocephalians Amtocephale and Graciliceratops, and the hadrosauroid Gobihadros.
In 2009, Longrich and Currie suggested that unlike specialized dromaeosaurids, Achillobator retained a conservative lifestyle and filled the niche of a large predator hunting medium to large prey.
Achillobator is classified within the subfamily Eudromaeosauria, a group of terrestrial, hypercarnivorous dromaeosaurids.
It is also classified within the family Dromaeosauridae and the subclade Eudromaeosauria, a group of obligate terrestrial and hypercarnivorous dinosaurs known as "true dromaeosaurids".
Achillobator lived during the late Cretaceous period, approximately between 93 and 80 million years ago, spanning the Turonian to Campanian stages.
Burnham and colleagues in 2000 suggested that the Achillobator holotype might be a paleontological chimera where only the foot claws belong to a dromaeosaurid.
The phylogenetic position of Achillobator is debated, with some studies placing it in the subfamily Dromaeosaurinae while others place it in Velociraptorinae.
Peter Mackovicky suggested that while sickle claws might have been used for climbing in primitive dromaeosaurids, giant animals like Achillobator were likely too large to climb trees effectively.
Peter Mackovicky suggested that larger dromaeosaurids adapted their sickle claws exclusively for aggressive predatory behavior.
